shortDescription: Nordic forward power prices rose to their highest in a week on Monday, buoyed by a growing hydro deficit that outweighed wetter-than-normal weather forecasts, while higher prices across European energy markets provided additional support.

children: Nordic forward power prices rose to their highest in a week on Monday, buoyed by a growing hydro deficit that outweighed wetter-than-normal weather forecasts, while higher prices across European energy markets provided additional support.
Nordic front-quarter baseload power contract (NSBLQc1) rose €4.2, or 4.92%, to €89.6 per megawatt hour (MWh) at 1222 GMT. Prices were down 4.9% so far for the month.
Nordic front-year (NSBLYc1) gained €1.55, or 2.81%, to €56.75 per megawatt hour. It is on track for its second straight monthly rise, up 2.8% so far.
"The next few weeks look somewhat wetter than seasonal average, but not enough to erase the deficit on the Nordic hydro balance as we head into autumn," analysts at Mind Energy said in a note.
Nordic water reserves available 15 days ahead (PCAEC00) were seen at 10.68 terawatt hours (TWh) below normal, versus 10.26 TWh below normal on Friday.
"Atlantic low pressure activity will continue to dominate the weather in Northern Europe this week, and likely also next week," said LSEG meteorologist Georg Muller.
"Next week appears to be similar with no signs of stable dry and warmer weather before mid-September," Muller said.
German day-ahead power prices rose as wind and to a lesser extent solar power generation fell, while consumption was expected to rise.
Germany's year-ahead power (TRDEBYc1), Europe's benchmark contract, rose €2.1, or 1.83%, to €117.05 per MWh.

Benchmark Dutch wholesale gas rose as fresh attacks by the U.S. and Iran dashed hopes that liquefied natural gas flows would resume through the Strait of Hormuz ahead of the northern hemisphere winter, raising the risk of price increases.
